blocks.text: Your task is to take a focused history, determine medical eligibility, explain the method and provide accurate instructions for initiation and missed doses.
Model introduction

“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I understand you would like to discuss the progestogen-only contraceptive pill. I will ask a few questions about your health, menstrual cycle, pregnancy plans and any medicines you take. I will then explain how the pill works, how to take it and what to do if you miss a dose. Is that alright?”
Maintain privacy, obtain consent and invite questions. Explain that the patient may choose another suitable contraceptive method if she prefers.
Use the mnemonic MINI PILL.

blocks.text: Unlike the combined pill, POP does not contain oestrogen and is generally suitable for many patients with conditions that make oestrogen-containing contraception inappropriate. However, current breast cancer is an important contraindication to hormonal contraception, and severe active liver disease may also affect eligibility.
Ask whether the patient is breastfeeding and how long ago she delivered.

POP is generally compatible with breastfeeding and is often a useful postpartum option. The appropriate start time and backup requirements depend on the formulation, timing since delivery and whether another method was used.

blocks.text: These windows are formulation-specific. Always check the actual product and local prescribing guidance.
The POP works mainly through two mechanisms.
1. Thickening of cervical mucus
Progestogen makes cervical mucus less penetrable to sperm, reducing the likelihood of sperm reaching the upper reproductive tract.
2. Suppression of ovulation
Ovulation is suppressed consistently with some formulations, particularly desogestrel and drospirenone, but not in every cycle with traditional POP formulations.
3. Endometrial changes
Progestogen changes the endometrium, but this is not the main contraceptive mechanism.
Unlike combined hormonal contraception, POP contains no oestrogen. It does not provide protection against sexually transmitted infections.

content_groups.group_title: Step 1: Exclude pregnancy when reasonably possible

blocks.text: Ask about the LMP, recent intercourse and current contraceptive use. Use a pregnancy test when indicated, recognising that a negative test may not detect a very recent conception.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2: Start at the appropriate time

blocks.text: Many POP formulations can be started immediately if pregnancy can reasonably be excluded.

The need for backup contraception depends on the formulation and timing of initiation. For many traditional or desogestrel POPs, starting during the first five days of menstrual bleeding does not require backup. Starting later usually requires condoms or abstinence for two days. Drospirenone has different initiation rules; starting outside the recommended early-cycle window generally requires seven days of backup.
Always confirm the specific product's instructions.

items.text: Take one pill every day.
Take it at a consistent time, particularly with traditional POP.
Start the next pack immediately after completing the previous pack.
Do not create a routine pill-free interval unless the specific formulation's instructions require a different regimen.

blocks.text: Explain expected bleeding changes, missed-pill instructions, drug interactions, STI prevention and how to obtain help if adverse effects become troublesome.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Missed POP: the essential OSCE algorithm

blocks.text: First identify the formulation. Never apply the same missed-pill rule to every mini-pill.

blocks.title: If the pill is more than three hours late:

items.text: Take the missed pill as soon as you remember.
Take the next pill at the usual time, even if this means taking two pills on the same day.
Use condoms or abstain from intercourse until pills have been taken correctly for 48 hours.
Assess whether emergency contraception is required if unprotected intercourse occurred during the period of reduced protection.

blocks.title: If the pill is more than 12 hours late:

items.text: Take the most recently missed pill as soon as possible.
Continue the remaining pills at the usual time.
Use condoms or abstain from intercourse until the pill has been taken correctly for 48 hours.
Assess the need for emergency contraception based on the timing of intercourse and missed doses.

blocks.text: Drospirenone 4 mg is commonly supplied in a 24-active/4-inactive tablet regimen.
Its missed-pill instructions differ from those of traditional and desogestrel POPs. In general:

items.text: A single active pill taken late or missed for less than 48 hours since it should have been taken can usually be taken as soon as possible, without additional contraception.
If two or more consecutive active pills are missed, take the most recently missed active pill, continue the pack and use backup contraception for seven days.
If missed pills occur near the end of the active-tablet sequence, follow the product-specific instructions for managing the inactive-tablet interval.

blocks.text: Because drospirenone packs contain inactive tablets, distinguish a missed active tablet from a missed placebo tablet.

columns: Typical backup after a qualifying missed pill
rows: Usually 7 days after two or more consecutive active pills are missed

blocks.text: These are general teaching rules; product leaflets and national guidance should take precedence where they differ.
Examiner's question: A woman taking desogestrel 75 micrograms remembers her pill 15 hours late. What will you advise?

Model answer: I would advise her to take the most recently missed pill immediately, continue the pack at the usual time, and use condoms or abstain for the next 48 hours. I would establish whether she had unprotected intercourse during the period of reduced protection and assess whether emergency contraception is needed.
If vomiting occurs soon after taking a pill, absorption may be incomplete. The relevant time window varies by formulation and product.

Severe or prolonged diarrhoea can also reduce reliability. Follow the product-specific missed-pill instructions, use backup contraception when indicated, and assess pregnancy risk if unprotected intercourse has occurred.
Examples include rifampicin, rifabutin, carbamazepine and phenytoin. These can reduce the effectiveness of some oral hormonal contraceptives.
A copper IUD or an appropriate hormonal IUD may be a better option when enzyme induction is expected to compromise oral contraception.

content_groups.group_title: E. Wants rapid return to fertility

blocks.text: Explain that fertility generally returns rapidly after stopping POP. It does not ordinarily cause permanent infertility.

blocks.text: Q1. What is the main difference between POP and COCP?
POP contains only a progestogen, whereas COCP contains both oestrogen and progestogen. POP is generally suitable for many women who cannot use oestrogen-containing contraception.
Q2. Why must traditional POP be taken at a consistent time?
Its permitted late-pill window is only three hours. Delayed doses may compromise contraceptive protection because the formulation does not consistently suppress ovulation.
Q3. What is the missed-pill window for desogestrel POP?
Twelve hours. If the pill is more than 12 hours late, the patient should follow the missed-pill instructions, including 48 hours of backup contraception in the usual regimen.
Q4. What is the most common counselling issue with POP?
Unpredictable bleeding, which may present as spotting, irregular bleeding, infrequent menstruation or amenorrhoea.
Q5. Can POP be used during breastfeeding?
Generally, yes. It is a commonly used postpartum method, subject to individual eligibility and the relevant formulation's initiation instructions.
Q6. Does POP prevent sexually transmitted infections?
No. Condoms are needed when STI protection is required.
Q7. Does POP cause permanent infertility?
No. Fertility generally returns rapidly after discontinuation.
Q8. What should you do if a patient misses pills and had unprotected intercourse?

Establish the formulation, number of missed active pills and timing of intercourse. Give the appropriate missed-pill instructions, assess whether emergency contraception is indicated, and arrange pregnancy testing when appropriate.
